9.0.0.en: When a person's affairs are settled, he often forgets God and the doing of good. David, however, with his great heart, once he was settled began to seek to do good even to the one who had been most hostile to him, King Saul. He did not forget the covenant he had made with Saul (1 Sam 24:20-22), and likewise with his son Jonathan, to care for their descendants (1 Sam 20:12-17). Out of his love for Jonathan he sought to fulfill his promise, and so he asked those around him whether anyone of the house of Saul was still alive.

9.0.1.en: Because David was a king appointed by God, he did not act like the other kings of the world, who destroy the offspring of the kings before them. And here we see how the love and care that Jonathan had sown toward David, and his protecting him when Saul wanted to kill him, God repaid to him through David's care for his son Mephibosheth.

9.0.2.en: Do not forget your covenants with God and with people. If God is faithful in His covenant with you to care for you, why are you negligent in your covenants and in keeping His commandments? He loves you, so renew your covenants with Him to the measure that suits you, in specific exercises; and if you tend to forget, write down your covenants with God and with people so that you may carry them out.

9.1.0.en: David's men set about searching for someone who could tell them news of the house of Saul and who of them remained alive. They came to a servant of the house of Saul whose name was “Ziba,” and they ordered him to come before David, who asked him whether he was “Ziba,” and he answered that he was.

9.2.0.en: The king asked him whether anyone of the house of Saul was still alive, that he might show him kindness. Ziba answered him that there was a son of Jonathan who was lame in both feet (he is Mephibosheth, who was mentioned in ch. 4:4).

9.2.1.en: Every good deed we do for others is in truth directed to God Himself, as the Lord Christ said: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mt 25:40).

9.3.0.en: Lo-debar: a place in Gilead, called Debir in (Josh 10:38), and now known as Umm ad-Dabar, south of Wadi al-Arab, east of the Jordan.

9.3.1.en: David asked him where he could find this son, and he answered that he was in the house of “Machir the son of Ammiel,” in the land of Gilead. This man was noble in hiding Mephibosheth with him so that no one would harm him, and he must have done so out of loyalty to Saul. He was also loyal to David, for he honored David and his men when they came to Mahanaim in flight from his son Absalom, who had risen in revolt against him (ch. 17:27-29).

9.4.0.en: David sent messengers to the house of Machir to bring Mephibosheth from there to him in Jerusalem. Saul had other sons and grandsons, such as his sons by Rizpah and his grandsons by Merab (1 Chr 8:33), but Ziba did not mention them. We do not know Mephibosheth's feelings when he was summoned: was he afraid of some harm intended for him by David, or did he believe what he had heard from Ziba, that David wished to do him good? In any case, he had to go to David.

9.5.0.en: Mephibosheth came to David and showed his great respect and submission to him, for he bowed down before him and declared his complete readiness to obey him, saying, “Behold thy servant!”

9.6.0.en: Saul thy father: a grandfather is counted as a father to his grandchildren.

9.6.1.en: David reassured him and made him understand that his purpose in bringing him was to show him kindness, in faithfulness to his friendship with his father Jonathan. Mephibosheth did not know of the friendly relationship that had existed between his father and David, for he was only five years old when his father died. David also promised to restore to him all the lands of his grandfather Saul, which had passed to David after the death of Ishbosheth and the return of Michal to him as wife. And to honor him further, he ordered that he should eat his food at the king's table as one of his own household.

9.7.0.en: Mephibosheth had not expected this generous treatment from David, and he could do nothing but bow down a second time in thanks and appreciation, for he had thought himself a nobody after the kingship had departed from the house of Saul, and he likened himself to a dead dog, which has no strength and no use.

9.7.1.en: Long before, David had bowed down to Jonathan as heir to the throne in the days of the kingship of his father Saul (1 Sam 20:41); and now God restores honor to the humble David, so that the son of Jonathan bows down to him.

9.7.2.en: Does this expression not call for some reflection here? Is it not the very same expression, “a dead dog,” that David used when he was being hunted by Saul (1 Sam 24:14)? The days turn, and the grandson of Saul says it to David! But David had said it in great humility despite his strength and despite Saul having fallen into his hands, whereas Mephibosheth says it in the face of David's gifts and his love that surpasses understanding.

9.7.3.en: Be humble and thankful to everyone who honors you, for thanks is the least thing that can be offered to the generous. And thank God, who has made people honor you.

9.8.0.en: Thou shalt till: that is, you shall plow the land and sow it.

9.8.1.en: Bring in the fruits: that is, bring forth produce from the land.

9.8.2.en: David gave his instructions to Ziba. He first informed him that he had granted to Mephibosheth, his master, all that had belonged to Saul of agricultural lands, on condition that Ziba, the members of his household and his servants should cultivate the land and look after it so that it would yield abundant crops, providing food and the other needs for Mephibosheth and his household; and he also decreed that Mephibosheth should eat his food at the king's table. It appears from this verse that Ziba was the head of a large household, for he had fifteen sons, besides daughters, as well as twenty servants, all of whom were able to look after the wide lands that David had given to Mephibosheth.

9.9.0.en: Ziba promised King David that he would carry out everything he had commanded him exactly. And David added the following statement, confirming his honoring of Mephibosheth, that he should always eat at the king's table as one of his sons.

9.10.0.en: Micha: the son of Mephibosheth and grandson of Jonathan. His name appears as the son of “Merib-baal” in (1 Chr 8:

9.10.1.en: 34), and likewise in (1 Chr 9:40), who is Mephibosheth himself.

9.10.2.en: The inspired text mentions here a son of Mephibosheth, Micha, who is mentioned again in (1 Chr 8:35-39) and (1 Chr 9:41-44) as head of a clan among the clans of Benjamin. And (1 Chr 8:40) adds that among his descendants there were mighty men of valor, strong in wars, who had many sons and grandsons. In accordance with the king's command, all the members of Ziba's household and his servants obeyed and served Mephibosheth in all the property and lands that were restored to him. This lasted for a time, and then Ziba turned against Mephibosheth afterward, as the inspired text will tell us, and falsely slandered him to the king (ch. 16:1-4, 19:24-30).

9.11.0.en: From that time Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem so as to be near King David, who regarded him as one of his own circle who ate at his table. The lands of his grandfather Saul that David restored to him were in Gibeah of Benjamin, and Ziba tended them and brought their produce to him. And as we learned in (ch. 4:4), Mephibosheth was lame in both feet as a result of his nurse fleeing with him and dropping him from her hand to the ground, and he remained so all his life.

9.11.1.en: Reflect on God's gifts to you, so that you may trust in His care and your heart may be at peace, and you may feel how very beloved you are to His heart; then you will reject every sin and live for Him, enjoying fellowship with Him.

9.11.2.en: David's victories over the Ammonites and the Arameans

10.0.s.en: (1) The insult of the king of Ammon to David

10.0.0.en: The children of Ammon: they are the descendants of Lot, and they dwell east of the Jordan River, and there were many wars between them and the children of Israel. Nahash, their king, was a friend of David because of the hostility of both toward Saul. Nahash king of the Ammonites, who had been hostile to the children of Israel, died; Saul had confronted him and defeated him (1 Sam 11). After his death his son Hanun reigned in his place.

10.1.0.en: It seems that Nahash king of the Ammonites had done some good to David, perhaps when David was fleeing from Saul; so when Nahash died, David sent messengers to console his son Hanun, who reigned after him.

10.2.0.en: Hanun's counselors suspected the messengers of David and told the king that they had come to spy out the land and learn its fortifications so that David might attack him, and that the purpose of their visit was not consolation.

10.3.0.en: Buttocks: the hinder part of the body, from behind.

10.3.1.en: Hanun rushed without wisdom after his counselors, and he insulted David's messengers and despised them by shaving off half of their beards and cutting off their garments from behind up to the buttocks, to mock David and his people.

10.4.0.en: David's messengers were in great shame at the insult that had come upon them, and they sent to David to tell him what Hanun had done to them. King David was greatly displeased at this foolish conduct on the part of Hanun, and he sent them new garments and told them to remain at Jericho until their beards had grown again, and then to return to Jerusalem.

10.4.1.en: Do not rush after any counsel you hear, however close the counselors may be to you, for they may sometimes lack wisdom. Examine the matter, seek God's guidance, and return to your father and spiritual guide, and you will always act wisely.

10.5.0.en: They stank before David: David hated them because of what they had done.

10.5.1.en: Beth-rehob (Aram): a small Aramean state near Hamath, in the upper Jordan valley in northern Palestine, near Dan.

10.5.2.en: Aram-zobah or Zobah: a small Aramean state west of the Euphrates, which belonged to King Hadadezer (ch. 8:3). Maacah: this is Aram-maacah, a small Aramean state east of the Jordan near Mount Hermon. Tob: a region east of the Jordan.

10.5.3.en: The children of Ammon felt that their insult to the messengers whom David had sent must have angered him and that David would surely punish them, so they prepared armies for the war that David might wage against them. Since they were weaker than David in military strength, they hired soldiers from the surrounding Aramean peoples, and the numbers of those soldiers were as follows:

10.5.4.en: 20 thousand footmen from Beth-rehob and Zoba, a thousand men from Maacah, and 12 thousand men from Tob. And in (1 Chr 19) we find other details about the preparations of the king of the Ammonites, namely that he hired a large number of horsemen and war chariots, and that the king of Maacah went out himself to fight with him.

10.6.0.en: David took note of the Ammonites' preparation of armies, so he in turn commissioned the commander of his army, Joab, to summon the chosen, mighty men of war to meet the armies of the children of Ammon and those with them.

10.7.0.en: The children of Ammon arranged their ranks according to a plan they had devised to surprise David's armies with: the Ammonites drew up at the entrance of their capital “Rabbah” to meet David's armies if they came from the north, while the Arameans drew up in the plain east of the Dead Sea to confront David's armies if they came from the south.

10.8.0.en: Joab found two parties ready to attack him, the hired Arameans from the north and the Ammonites dwelling in Rabbah from the south. So he drew up his plan to match the plan that the children of Ammon had laid down: he also divided his army into two parts, each part facing a part of the enemy's armies. He himself led the chosen, that is the strongest, part, which had to face the hired Arameans because they were the stronger party, while he assigned his brother Abishai to command the part that had to face the Ammonites.

10.9.0.en: Joab agreed with his brother Abishai that each of them would watch the other's position in the battle, so that if the fighting position of one of them was in danger, the other would come to his aid.

10.10.0.en: Joab encouraged his younger brother Abishai, stressing in his words the need to endure and to fight with courage for the sake of the victory of their people and the preservation of its honor among the nations, and in defense of the land that the Lord had given them. They must strive as far as they were able, and the Lord would complete the rest.

10.10.1.en: If the forces of the enemy devil attack us and we feel that the war against us is fierce, let us strive and resist him, firmly grounded in faith in the word of the Lord, who gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.

10.11.0.en: Joab attacked the Arameans, and with God's help the Arameans were afraid of him and fled. This terrified the children of Ammon, for if the mighty Arameans had fled, what would the armies of the children of Israel do to them? So they were very afraid and fled before them.

10.12.0.en: When the news of the flight of the Arameans before David reached the Ammonites, their allies in the war, their morale weakened and they were certain that they could not stand alone after the Arameans' withdrawal from the field of battle. So they too decided to withdraw before Abishai and retreated into their city “Rabbah of Ammon” in order to reorder their ranks, for after a year they attacked the children of Israel, as is recorded in (ch. 11). And when Joab saw that the enemies had scattered and fled from the fight, he returned rejoicing in the victory to Jerusalem, and perhaps David sang at that time Psalms 2, 20, 21, and 110.

10.13.0.en: The Arameans did not accept the defeat that the people of Israel had inflicted on them, so they decided to gather their military forces again and to bring other Aramean states into their ranks so as to increase the numbers of their armies.

10.14.0.en: He brought out the Arameans beyond the River: he placed them at the front of the armies because of their courage.

10.14.1.en: Aram beyond the River is the name by which the Hebrews called Aram-naharaim (Naharaim, “the two rivers,” referring to the Tigris and the Euphrates). Helam: a place east of the Jordan.

10.14.2.en: Shobach: the commander of the army of Hadadezer, king of Aram-zobah and the greatest of the kings of the Arameans.

10.14.3.en: Hadadezer was the leader of the effort to reconstitute the armies. He had previously fought a battle against David in which he was also defeated (ch. 8:3), so he sought vengeance for his earlier defeats before David. He therefore summoned the Arameans dwelling between the Tigris and the Euphrates and placed them at the front of his armies because they were famous for courage and strength, and he appointed “Shobach,” the commander-in-chief of Hadadezer's army, to lead them, and these armies drew up at “Helam.”

10.15.0.en: The news of the movements of the Aramean armies and their preparations reached David, so he decided to lead the army of Israel himself and to take the initiative in the war. He crossed the Jordan River and came with his armies to “Helam,” and the two parties made ready for battle.

10.16.0.en: Once again the Lord gave victory to Israel: David slew the soldiers of seven hundred chariots, each chariot carrying ten soldiers, and he also slew 40 thousand horsemen and footmen, as well as “Shobach” the commander of the enemy's armies.

10.16.1.en: It is mentioned in (1 Chr 19:18) that he slew 40 thousand footmen, while here it is 40 thousand horsemen. Each writer saw the part most important in his view and ascribed the whole to it: in 2 Samuel the forty thousand are ascribed to the horsemen although they were of both horsemen and footmen, and the opposite in the First Book of Chronicles, which ascribes them to the footmen.

10.17.0.en: When it became clear to the Aramean kings, who had originally joined under the banner of their supreme king Hadadezer, that they had not the strength to stand against the people of Israel, they made peace with them, by which they acknowledged submission to Israel, and no longer responded to any request from the Ammonites to ally with them in any wars against the children of Israel. And by the victory over the Arameans and their subjection to the children of Israel, the borders of David's kingdom extended to the Euphrates, fulfilling God's promise to Abraham that his descendants would possess the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates (Gen 15:18); and what is meant by the Nile is the seasonal river east of the wilderness of Sinai, that is, west of the Philistines, whom David defeated.

10.17.1.en: If troubles multiply upon you, or many gather against you, do not be alarmed, for your God is stronger than all the world and is able to deliver you and give you victory over them. Hold fast to Him with much prayer and persistence, and you will receive His power, which is able to do all things.
